content: The World Health Organization (WHO) explicitly states that the designations and presentation of material in its publications do not imply any opinion regarding the legal status of any country, territory, city, or area, nor do they imply any stance on the delimitation of frontiers or boundaries. Any dotted or dashed lines on maps are approximate and may not reflect full agreement on borders. The mention of specific companies or products does not constitute endorsement or recommendation by WHO over others of a similar nature. Proprietary product names are distinguished by initial capital letters. WHO has taken all reasonable precautions to verify the information in its publications. However, the material is distributed without any warranty, expressed or implied. The responsibility for interpreting and using the material lies with the reader, and WHO is not liable for any damages arising from its use. In 2012, Oman became the first country to be recognized as having eliminated trachoma as a public health problem. This process was referred to as a verification exercise. In 2015, the WHO Strategic and Technical Advisory Group on Neglected Tropical Diseases endorsed standardized processes for confirming and acknowledging success in eliminating neglected tropical diseases. For diseases targeted for elimination as a public health problem, this process is termed validation. The validation process for trachoma elimination involves a two-step approach. First, after implementing interventions and at least six months following the final round of mass antibiotic administration, an impact survey is conducted. If the prevalence threshold for trachomatous inflammation-follicular (TF) is met, the district enters a two-year pre-validation surveillance period during which no further mass antibiotic administration is conducted. At the end of this period, a pre-validation surveillance survey is undertaken. Standard operating procedures for these surveys are provided separately. A country meets the criteria for validation if all previously endemic districts demonstrate sub-elimination threshold prevalence levels for trachomatous trichiasis (TT) and TF in adequately conducted pre-validation surveillance surveys. Consideration may also be given to the timing of interventions and surveillance activities in adjacent districts. The Member State must prepare a dossier documenting the achievement of elimination targets, which may include assistance from WHO. The dossier should follow the template established by WHO and be submitted in both hard and electronic copies to the WHO Country Office, which will forward it to the relevant regional and headquarters offices. The dossier is assessed by an ad-hoc Dossier Review Group, which evaluates the evidence and recommends whether the claim of elimination should be validated. The group is appointed by the WHO Regional Office in consultation with the Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases at WHO headquarters. The group comprises experts in the SAFE strategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness, and Environmental improvement) and validation processes, ensuring no conflicts of interest with the Member State under review. The group may recommend validation, postponement, or additional evidence to support the claim. Recommendations must be justified and may include guidance on post-validation surveillance or steps for future validation. The Secretariat supports the group by providing dossiers, organizing discussions, and facilitating country visits if necessary. All group members must maintain confidentiality and provide independent reviews of the dossier. If the group recommends validation, the summary report is forwarded to the Director of the Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases at WHO headquarters, who notifies the WHO Director-General. If validation is postponed, the report is sent to the Member State. WHO may report the achievement in its publications and update the trachoma endemicity status in the Global Health Observatory. Validation is reversible, and countries must continue post-validation surveillance as recommended. Surveillance data should be reported to WHO, and any recrudescence above elimination thresholds will be noted in the Global Health Observatory and the Weekly Epidemiological Record. With the Member State's agreement, validated dossiers may be made publicly available on the WHO website as reference documents.
